title: Steel Studs: Save on Labor and Build Smarter in 2026
description: Complete 2026 guide to steel studs and metal framing: gauges, spans, clips, tracks, and best practices from Dass Metal Products in Vaughan, ON.
html:
Last updated: October 2026

Key takeaway:

Steel studs are cold-formed, galvanized framing members used with tracks and accessories to create straight, durable interior, exterior, and load-bearing wall systems. Choose the profile, thickness, depth, spacing, and movement details from the wall height, loads, deflection limit, fire or acoustic assembly, and applicable code requirements – not from gauge alone.

By Dass Metal Products Editorial Team · Last updated: October 24, 2026

Steel studs give contractors a repeatable way to frame walls, bulkheads, shaft systems, furring assemblies, and structural partitions. Unlike wood, cold-formed steel does not warp, twist, rot, or provide food for pests. Galvanized coatings help protect the material from corrosion, while precision-formed webs and flanges support consistent layout and clean drywall finishes.

Dass Metal Products manufactures and supplies steel studs, tracks, channels, clips, and finishing components from Vaughan, Ontario. Its Canadian-made product range supports interior and exterior framing, including light-gauge non-loadbearing work and heavier structural metal stud applications. The company also provides product brochures, load tables, standards information, and technical support for projects across Canada and the United States.

What are steel studs?

Steel studs are cold-formed sections made by rolling galvanized sheet steel into a C-shaped profile. The stud normally sits inside a U-shaped track at the floor and head of a wall. Screws, clips, bridging, channels, sheathing, gypsum board, and insulation complete the assembly.

Interior non-loadbearing studs are commonly used for partitions, corridors, tenant improvements, bulkheads, and furring. Heavier cold-formed steel studs can be designed for axial, wind, and lateral loads in structural walls, exterior curtain-wall infill, and taller partitions. The same basic system can therefore serve very different purposes, but the correct profile must be selected for the specific assembly.

  • Web: the broad central face of the stud, often containing factory-punched service holes.
  • Flanges: the sides that receive screws and support gypsum board or sheathing.
  • Returns or lips: formed edges that improve stiffness and help maintain the profile.
  • Track: a channel-shaped member that receives the ends of studs and establishes the wall line.
  • Accessories: clips, bridging channel, deflection track, furring channel, resilient channel, trims, and angles that complete the system.

Nominal gauge is not a sufficient specification by itself. The designer or specifier should identify the actual design thickness, stud depth, yield strength where relevant, coating, spacing, connection method, and required load or span information. A manufacturer’s load tables and project drawings should control the final selection.

Which standards and Ontario code requirements apply?

In Ontario, the current framework is the 2024 Building Code under Ontario Regulation 163/24, effective January 1, 2025, with later amendments identified in the current provincial compendium. The Ontario 2024 Building Code Compendium is the appropriate starting point for administrative, technical, fire, and structural requirements.

Structural cold-formed steel design must follow the requirements identified by the applicable code and referenced standards. Ontario’s structural provisions state that buildings and structural members made of cold-formed steel are to conform to CSA S136, the North American Specification for the Design of Cold-Formed Steel Structural Members, using the Canadian provisions. The Ontario structural design provisions should be reviewed by the project’s qualified designer for structural applications.

The Ontario code also distinguishes between structural design, fire performance, material properties, and installation details. For non-loadbearing fire-rated assemblies, the fire-performance guidance includes requirements such as a clearance between the top of the stud and top runner where expansion in a fire must be accommodated. Review the relevant Ontario fire performance guidance and the tested assembly details rather than applying a generic wall recipe.

Specifications may also reference Division 05 requirements. The National Research Council’s current National Master Specification sections identify structural metal stud framing under Section 05 41 00. A project specification, architectural drawings, structural drawings, fire-rated assembly listing, and manufacturer data should be read together.

Why use steel studs for metal framing?

Steel studs are useful when dimensional consistency, noncombustibility, moisture resistance, and predictable installation matter. A straight stud helps maintain door jambs, millwork lines, tile planes, and drywall reveals. Because members are manufactured to repeatable dimensions, crews can establish a consistent layout across long corridors and multiple floors.

Dimensional stability

Wood can crown, twist, shrink, or swell as moisture conditions change. Steel does not behave in the same way, so it can reduce the correction work that appears when finishes are installed over uneven framing. It is still important to protect members from prolonged exposure to water and to specify suitable coatings for the environment.

Fire and moisture considerations

Steel framing is noncombustible, but a steel stud by itself does not create a fire-rated wall. The complete tested assembly – including stud thickness, spacing, board layers, fasteners, insulation, joints, and head-of-wall treatment – determines the rating. Similarly, galvanized steel resists corrosion, but wet service conditions may require a specified coating, separation of dissimilar metals, drainage, and additional protection.

Coordination and productivity

Factory-punched holes can simplify routing for electrical, plumbing, and low-voltage services. Bundling members by wall type or construction zone also makes procurement and floor staging easier. These benefits depend on accurate drawings, correct lengths, and a material schedule that includes tracks, clips, bridging, trims, fasteners, and replacement pieces.

What types of steel studs and components are available?

A metal framing system is more than a row of studs. Each component responds to a particular structural, movement, acoustic, finishing, or coordination requirement.

Non-loadbearing studs

Light-gauge non-loadbearing studs are used for interior partitions, framed ceilings, bulkheads, and furring. The selected depth may be 2-1/2, 3-5/8, 6, or another project-specific dimension. Spacing is often 16 or 24 inches on centre, but the drawings and assembly listing control.

Load-bearing and structural studs

Heavy-gauge studs are used where the wall carries axial or lateral loads or supports exterior cladding. Structural design must account for compression, bending, combined loading, local buckling, connection capacity, bridging, openings, and the supporting structure. Dass Metal’s load-bearing stud framing system information can help a project team identify the type of product data needed before ordering.

Tracks and deflection components

Standard track holds the base and head of a fixed partition. Deep track can provide additional leg depth or tolerance where the design requires it. Slotted deflection track allows a wall to remain laterally restrained while accommodating vertical movement from a slab or roof above. Deflection clips and web-slide clips can provide a similar movement function when specified for the assembly.

Bridging and channels

Bridging channel and carrying channel help control stud rotation and out-of-plane movement, particularly in taller walls. Resilient channel separates gypsum board from the framing to interrupt vibration paths. Furring channel and Z-bar can level an uneven substrate, create a service cavity, or support a finish system.

Trims and finishing pieces

J trim, L trim, J track, cornerbead, utility angles, flat strips, hanger wire, and tie wire address edges, corners, transitions, and support conditions. A complete takeoff should include these small items because omitting them can create field substitutions and delay board installation.

How should you choose gauge, depth, and spacing?

Select steel studs by starting with the wall’s use and design conditions. Identify whether the wall is non-loadbearing or structural, establish its height, determine the board and insulation layers, define the required deflection limit, and check the loads applied to the wall. Then select a profile and spacing using the manufacturer’s data or the project engineer’s design.

Design questionWhy it mattersWhat to confirm
Is the wall loadbearing?Structural walls require more than a partition rule of thumb.Axial, wind, lateral, opening, connection, and bracing design.
How tall is the wall?Height increases bending and deflection demands.Stud depth, thickness, spacing, bridging, and span data.
What finish is attached?Board layers, tile, cladding, and cabinets add weight or stiffness demands.Fastener capacity, backing, board orientation, and assembly listing.
Can the structure move?Slab or roof deflection can crack finishes or load a partition.Head-of-wall gap, slotted track, clips, and movement allowance.
Is the wall rated or acoustic?Performance belongs to the complete tested or designed assembly.Listed layers, spacing, insulation, channels, joints, and penetrations.

Gauge numbers can be confusing because different product systems and manufacturers may describe thickness differently. Specify the actual mil or millimetre thickness, profile, depth, and design properties in the submittal. For example, a nominal 20-gauge product should not be treated as interchangeable with every other product labelled 20 gauge.

Spacing also affects performance and material quantity. Sixteen-inch centres may be selected for greater stiffness or heavier finishes, while 24-inch centres may be appropriate for a specific non-loadbearing assembly. Neither spacing should be assumed without checking the wall type, board system, fastener schedule, and design requirements.

What is the correct steel stud installation sequence?

Good installation begins with coordinated drawings and a material package. Before framing starts, confirm wall lines, openings, slab conditions, control joints, deflection requirements, service routes, and locations requiring backing. The field team should have the correct track, stud, clip, bridging, fastener, and trim schedule available by zone.

  1. Verify layout: establish wall lines, openings, intersections, and finished-face dimensions. Confirm that door swings, casework, shafts, and equipment clearances work together.
  2. Install base track: anchor the track using the specified fastener type and spacing. Check the substrate, edge distances, alignment, and transitions at corners.
  3. Install head track: use standard track for a fixed condition or the specified slotted track or clip system where vertical movement is expected.
  4. Cut and place studs: cut members to the required length, place them at the scheduled centres, and orient service holes consistently. Do not force a stud tightly into a deflection head condition.
  5. Frame openings: provide jamb studs, headers, reinforcement, and backing according to the drawings. Openings carrying loads require design-specific members and connections.
  6. Add bridging and clips: install bridging channel and clips at the required intervals. Confirm that bridging does not conflict with ducts, pipes, boxes, or access panels.
  7. Coordinate services: route services through punched holes where possible and protect sharp edges with approved grommets or bushings where required.
  8. Install board and accessories: follow the specified screw pattern, board orientation, joint arrangement, resilient-channel direction, trims, and sealants for the assembly.
  9. Inspect before concealment: check plumb, spacing, openings, backing, head-of-wall movement, fasteners, penetrations, and required documentation before closing the wall.

Do not weld, notch, drill, or remove flanges from structural members without design approval. Field changes can reduce capacity or invalidate a tested assembly. If a service route conflicts with the framing, resolve the conflict with the designer, engineer, or manufacturer rather than improvising at the wall.

How do deflection, fire, and acoustics affect the design?

Head-of-wall deflection

A partition beneath a concrete slab or long-span roof may experience vertical movement above it. If the head track is fixed tightly to the structure, that movement can transfer into studs, board, fasteners, and finishes. A slotted deflection track or compatible clip system creates the movement allowance shown in the design while preserving the required lateral support.

The gap is not a generic number. It depends on the anticipated movement, the product, the tested or engineered assembly, and the installation instructions. The field team should measure the actual condition and maintain the specified allowance continuously across the wall, including corners, intersections, and penetrations.

Fire-rated partitions

Steel studs contribute noncombustible framing, but the fire rating comes from the complete assembly. Use the listed board type, number of layers, fastener pattern, insulation, joint treatment, and head-of-wall detail. Ontario’s fire guidance identifies specific requirements for non-loadbearing cold-formed steel wall construction, so the applicable fire-performance provisions and tested design should be checked before installation.

Acoustic partitions

Sound performance depends on mass, cavity absorption, airtightness, and decoupling. Resilient channel can reduce direct vibration transfer between gypsum and framing, but incorrect orientation, fasteners that bridge the channel, unsealed penetrations, or poorly fitted doors can undermine the result. Use the complete tested or specified assembly and coordinate electrical boxes, pipes, ducts, and access panels.

What should a steel stud submittal include?

A useful submittal lets the reviewer verify that the proposed members match the drawings and specification. Organize the information by wall type instead of sending an undifferentiated product catalogue.

  • Product name, profile, depth, design thickness, coating, and material properties.
  • Load tables, span tables, and design assumptions for structural or tall-wall applications.
  • Track, clip, bridging, fastener, and connector compatibility.
  • Fire-rated and acoustic assembly references where those performance claims apply.
  • Installation instructions, service-hole limits, bracing requirements, and field modification restrictions.
  • Product standards, manufacturer certifications, safety documentation, and current technical data.
  • Packaging, lengths, quantities, delivery sequence, and any custom profile requirements.

For structural metal stud work, the structural metal stud construction guide provides a useful orientation to system components and design coordination. Teams planning broader interior applications can also review Dass Metal’s steel studs and metal framing overview.

Procurement should include waste, openings, damaged-member replacements, transitions, and accessory counts. Confirm whether the job needs standard lengths or custom profiles before fabrication. Dass Metal’s engineering team can help contractors and specifiers coordinate dimensions and quantities when the drawings include unusual geometries or tight delivery windows.

What should Vaughan projects plan for?

Projects supplied from the Vaughan area benefit from early coordination between the framing schedule, site storage, and delivery sequence. Steel bundles should be staged where lifting equipment can access them without blocking fire routes, loading zones, or other trades. Sorting studs and tracks by floor, elevation, or wall type can reduce unnecessary handling on busy Greater Toronto sites.

Winter conditions, changing site access, and occupied renovations can affect when materials can be unloaded and protected. Confirm the delivery window with the general contractor, keep members supported and reasonably protected from standing water, and verify that the site has enough laydown space for the planned bundle sizes.

For basement or renovation work, early service coordination is particularly valuable because existing concrete, masonry, and mechanical systems may limit standard wall dimensions. The basement steel stud framing guide offers a practical starting point for reviewing layout, moisture, and finishing considerations before mobilization.

Steel studs versus wood: which is better?

Neither material is automatically better for every project. Steel is often preferred where straightness, noncombustibility, repeatable dimensions, and moisture or pest resistance are priorities. Wood may be convenient for small residential work where local crews, field cutting, and readily available lumber dominate the decision.

FactorSteel studsWood studs
Dimensional stabilityConsistent and resistant to warp, rot, and pests.Can shrink, crown, twist, or swell with moisture changes.
Fire behaviorNoncombustible framing, subject to the complete rated assembly.Combustible framing that requires the specified protection.
Service coordinationOften includes punched holes and dedicated accessories.Easy to cut and drill, but field openings need careful placement.
Structural designRequires profile-specific cold-formed steel design data.Uses wood design values and connection requirements.
Field modificationCut with suitable snips or cutters; structural alterations need approval.Simple to saw, but excessive notching or drilling also reduces capacity.
Acoustic detailingWorks with resilient channel, furring, staggered, and other assemblies.Can also achieve acoustic performance with the specified assembly.

Mixed systems are common. For example, a wood structure may contain steel interior partitions, or steel framing may support a finish system attached to another structural material. At those interfaces, coordinate movement, fasteners, fire stopping, corrosion protection, and tolerances rather than treating each material as an isolated scope.

Steel stud field checklist

Use this checklist during design review, procurement, and pre-board inspection:

  • Identify each wall as non-loadbearing, loadbearing, shaft, furring, exterior, rated, or acoustic.
  • Record wall height, stud depth, design thickness, spacing, coating, and required deflection.
  • Confirm standard, deep, or slotted track and the compatible clips or connections.
  • Schedule bridging, backing, headers, jambs, and reinforcement before delivery.
  • Coordinate ducts, pipes, boxes, access panels, doors, casework, and equipment supports.
  • Match board, insulation, resilient channel, sealant, and fasteners to the specified assembly.
  • Check plumb, alignment, openings, fastener installation, head-of-wall gaps, and service penetrations.
  • Keep current product data, load tables, assembly listings, and inspection records with the project file.

For a broader overview of wall layout and product selection, see the steel stud wall framing guide. If an existing article or guide is used for orientation, the project drawings, current code, tested assembly, and manufacturer data still govern the installation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are steel studs used for?

Steel studs are used for interior partitions, corridors, bulkheads, shaft walls, furring, exterior infill, and engineered load-bearing walls. The required profile depends on the wall’s height, loads, finish, movement, fire, acoustic, and moisture conditions.

What gauge steel stud should I use for a 12-foot wall?

There is no safe universal gauge answer for a 12-foot wall. The designer must check stud depth, actual thickness, spacing, deflection, board layers, openings, loads, bridging, and the manufacturer’s span data. A product that works for one non-loadbearing partition may be unsuitable for another wall with cabinets, tile, or structural loading.

When is slotted deflection track required?

Slotted deflection track is used where the structure above can move vertically relative to a non-loadbearing wall, such as beneath a concrete slab or long-span roof. Use the product and movement allowance shown in the drawings or approved assembly, and do not fasten the stud in a way that prevents the intended movement.

Can steel studs be loadbearing?

Yes. Heavy-gauge cold-formed steel studs can form engineered load-bearing walls, but they require structural design for axial, bending, connection, opening, bracing, and support conditions. Review CSA S136-related design requirements and current manufacturer load tables before fabrication or ordering.
